objectives: Identify the structures of the outer, middle, and inner ear and their functions.
Explain how the ossicular chain achieves impedance matching between air and cochlear fluid.
Locate the cochlea and semicircular canals and state what each transduces.

slides.title: The outer ear: collecting and filtering sound
slides.body:
The auditory periphery is conventionally divided into three compartments: the **outer ear**, the **middle ear**, and the **inner ear**. Each performs a distinct physical job, and a fault in any one produces a characteristic kind of hearing loss. We begin at the surface.

The **outer ear** comprises the **pinna** (also called the **auricle**) and the **external auditory canal** (the ear canal), terminating at the **tympanic membrane** or eardrum. The pinna is the visible flap of elastic **cartilage** covered in skin. Far from being a passive funnel, its folds — the **helix**, **antihelix**, **concha**, and **tragus** — impose direction-dependent spectral filtering on incoming sound. These shape the **head-related transfer function (HRTF)** that the brain uses to judge whether a sound is in front, behind, above, or below. This is why a sound recorded with a dummy head and played over headphones can seem to come from a specific point in space.

The **ear canal** in an adult is roughly **2.5 cm long** and about 7-8 mm in diameter, running slightly upward and forward. Acoustically it behaves like a tube closed at one end (the eardrum), giving it a **quarter-wavelength resonance** near **3000-4000 Hz** that boosts sound pressure at the eardrum by **10-15 dB** in exactly the band most important for speech consonants. The canal also protects the delicate eardrum: its outer third secretes **cerumen** (earwax) from **ceruminous** and sebaceous glands, which traps debris, lubricates the skin, and is mildly antibacterial. The canal's slight S-shape and the lateral migration of skin cells form a self-cleaning conveyor.

The outer ear ends at the **tympanic membrane**, a thin, cone-shaped, three-layered membrane about 8-10 mm across and only about 0.1 mm thick. It is pulled inward at its center, the **umbo**, by the attached **manubrium** (handle) of the first middle-ear bone. Its larger lower part, the **pars tensa**, is taut and vibrates efficiently; the smaller upper **pars flaccida** is looser. When the canal's air pressure wave reaches the eardrum, the membrane moves like a piston, converting airborne acoustic energy into mechanical vibration. Disorders of the outer ear — a wax plug, a canal infection (**otitis externa**, sometimes called swimmer's ear), or a perforated eardrum — block or attenuate this airborne path and produce a **conductive** hearing loss without harming the inner ear's sensory cells.

slides.title: The middle ear and impedance matching
slides.body:
The **middle ear** is an air-filled cavity, the **tympanic cavity**, set in the **temporal bone** of the skull. It contains the three smallest bones in the human body, the **ossicles**, named for their shapes: the **malleus** (Latin for hammer), the **incus** (anvil), and the **stapes** (stirrup). They form an articulated chain. The malleus is fused to the inner surface of the tympanic membrane; it articulates with the incus, which in turn drives the stapes; and the **footplate** of the stapes seals into the **oval window**, the membrane-covered portal into the fluid-filled inner ear. The stapes is the smallest named bone in the human body, weighing only a few milligrams.

The middle ear solves a deep physics problem: **impedance matching**. Sound arrives in air, a light, springy medium of low **acoustic impedance**, but the inner ear is filled with **perilymph**, essentially salt water, which has impedance roughly 4000 times higher. When a wave passes from a low-impedance medium directly into a high-impedance one, almost all the energy reflects back. If sound struck the oval window directly, about **99.9 percent** of the energy would bounce off, a loss of about **30 dB**, and we would be functionally deaf. The middle ear acts as an acoustic transformer that recovers most of this energy through two mechanisms.

First and dominant is the **area ratio**. The vibrating area of the tympanic membrane (about **55 square millimeters** effective) is roughly **17 to 20 times** larger than the stapes footplate (about **3.2 square millimeters**). Because pressure equals force per unit area, concentrating the force collected over the large eardrum onto the tiny footplate multiplies the pressure by that ratio. Second is the **lever action** of the ossicular chain: the manubrium of the malleus is longer than the long process of the incus by a factor of about **1.3**, giving a modest mechanical advantage. Multiplying the area ratio by the lever ratio yields an overall pressure gain on the order of **22-fold**, near 27 dB, which very nearly recovers the 30 dB that would otherwise be lost. This is the elegant solution evolution found to push airborne sound into water.

Two other features deserve mention. The **Eustachian tube** (or pharyngotympanic tube) connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx; it is normally closed but opens on swallowing or yawning to equalize pressure across the eardrum (the cause of ear popping on aircraft). And two tiny muscles, the **tensor tympani** (innervated by the trigeminal nerve) and the **stapedius** (the smallest skeletal muscle in the body, innervated by the facial nerve), contract reflexively to stiffen the chain and attenuate loud sounds, the **acoustic reflex** that helps protect the inner ear and is itself a clinical test.

slides.title: The inner ear: cochlea and vestibular system
slides.body:
The **inner ear**, or **labyrinth**, is a complex of fluid-filled channels carved into the dense **petrous** part of the temporal bone. It serves two senses at once: **hearing**, via the **cochlea**, and **balance**, via the **vestibular system**. A bony outer shell (the **bony labyrinth**) houses a membranous inner tube (the **membranous labyrinth**) suspended in fluid. Two fluids matter: **perilymph**, similar to extracellular fluid (high sodium), fills the bony spaces, while **endolymph**, unusually rich in potassium, fills the membranous duct and is critical to sensory cell function.

The **cochlea** is a spiral tube coiled about two and three-quarter turns, resembling a snail shell (the Greek *kokhlias* means snail). Uncoiled it would be roughly **35 mm** long. In cross-section it shows three parallel chambers: the **scala vestibuli** above, the **scala tympani** below (both containing perilymph and joined at the apex through a small opening, the **helicotrema**), and between them the **scala media** or cochlear duct, which holds endolymph. The floor of the scala media is the **basilar membrane**, and resting on it is the sensory **organ of Corti**, named for **Alfonso Corti (1851)**, which carries the **hair cells** that convert vibration into neural signals. Sound vibrations entering at the **oval window** travel up the perilymph, deflect the basilar membrane, and are relieved at the round window, a second membrane-covered opening that bulges to accommodate the incompressible fluid.

Behind the cochlea sits the **vestibular system**, the organ of balance. It contains two **otolith organs**, the **utricle** and the **saccule**, whose hair cells are loaded with tiny calcium-carbonate crystals called **otoconia** that sense linear acceleration and the pull of gravity, telling you which way is down. It also contains the three **semicircular canals**, oriented roughly at right angles to one another in the horizontal, anterior, and posterior planes, so that together they detect rotational (angular) acceleration of the head about any axis. Each canal ends in a swelling, the **ampulla**, containing a sensory ridge, the **crista ampullaris**, whose hair cells project into a gelatinous **cupula** that is deflected when the endolymph lags behind a head turn.

Both the cochlear and vestibular hair cells feed the **vestibulocochlear nerve**, the **eighth cranial nerve (CN VIII)**, which carries auditory information along its cochlear division and balance information along its vestibular division to the brainstem. Because hearing and balance share this nerve, the same fluid spaces, and the same hair-cell technology, disorders such as **Meniere's disease** (an endolymph regulation problem first described by **Prosper Meniere** in 1861) can cause hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo together. Understanding which compartment is involved is the first diagnostic step every audiologist takes.

question.question: What is the **dominant** mechanism by which the middle ear matches the impedance of air to the impedance of cochlear fluid?
options: The Eustachian tube pressurizes the middle-ear cavity to push fluid.

The large effective area of the tympanic membrane (about 55 mm^2) concentrates collected force onto the much smaller stapes footplate (about 3.2 mm^2), an area ratio near 17-20 that multiplies pressure; a smaller ossicular lever adds a further ~1.3x.
The stapedius muscle amplifies vibrations by contracting on every sound.
The semicircular canals resonate at the incoming frequency and boost it.
question.explanation: The principal transformer action is the area ratio: pressure equals force per area, so funneling the force gathered over the broad eardrum onto the tiny stapes footplate raises pressure by roughly 17-20 times. The ossicular lever (about 1.3x) adds a smaller boost. Together they recover most of the ~30 dB that would be lost at a bare air-to-fluid interface. The Eustachian tube only equalizes static pressure, and the stapedius reflex attenuates rather than amplifies.

hints: Pressure equals force divided by area; compare the eardrum area to the footplate area.
The lever effect of the ossicles is real but small compared with the area effect.
slides.workedSolution: The middle ear is an acoustic transformer. Its dominant action is the area ratio: the effective tympanic membrane area (~55 mm^2) is about 17-20 times the stapes footplate area (~3.2 mm^2), so the force collected over the eardrum is concentrated to raise pressure by that factor. The ossicular lever adds about 1.3x. Combined, they regain most of the ~30 dB otherwise lost at the air-fluid boundary.

question.question: If the effective tympanic-membrane area is **55 mm^2** and the stapes footplate area is **3.2 mm^2**, what is the approximate **area ratio** (membrane to footplate)? Give a number rounded to the nearest whole value.
Localizing a lesion from symptoms.
question.prompt: A patient reports episodes of spinning vertigo, a roaring tinnitus, and fluctuating hearing loss in the left ear, all occurring together. Knowing that the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus share the inner-ear fluid spaces and the eighth cranial nerve, explain why a single disorder of endolymph regulation could produce all three symptoms at once, and name the classic condition this pattern suggests.

question.question: Which list correctly orders the three **ossicles** from the tympanic membrane to the oval window?
question.explanation: The malleus (hammer) is attached to the tympanic membrane, articulates with the incus (anvil), which drives the stapes (stirrup); the stapes footplate seals into the oval window. So the order from eardrum to inner ear is malleus, then incus, then stapes.

hints: The hammer strikes the anvil, which moves the stirrup.
The bone touching the eardrum is the malleus; the one in the oval window is the stapes.
slides.workedSolution: From the eardrum inward the chain is malleus (attached to the tympanic membrane), incus (the middle bone), then stapes (whose footplate enters the oval window). Hammer to anvil to stirrup.

question.question: Predicting the effect of a wax plug.
question.prompt: A patient comes in with a completely impacted plug of cerumen filling the left ear canal and a normal eardrum, middle ear, and cochlea behind it. Explain which compartment of the ear is affected, what type of hearing loss this produces, and why their sensory hair cells and balance organs are expected to be entirely normal.
